details:
**Bowen's reaction series**
Quartz sits at the very bottom of this sequence describing the order in which minerals crystallize from cooling magma, below muscovite and potassium feldspar. Because it has the lowest crystallization temperature, it is the last mineral to form, so it often fills the spaces between earlier crystals and lacks a well-formed crystal shape.

**Mohs hardness of 7**
Quartz defines the value of 7 on the Mohs scale of mineral hardness, between orthoclase feldspar (6) and topaz (8). This is one of the most common giveaways for the mineral.

**SiO2 (silicon dioxide, silica)**
The chemical formula of quartz: one silicon atom for every two oxygen atoms. Quartz is the most common crystalline form of silica and the main component of most sand.

**Piezoelectricity and crystal oscillators**
Quartz generates an electric voltage when mechanically stressed, and vibrates at a precise frequency when a voltage is applied. This makes it the basis of crystal oscillators that keep time in quartz watches and clocks and set frequencies in radio transmitters. George W. Pierce developed the Pierce oscillator circuit using quartz, and the cheaper ceramic PZT (lead zirconate titanate) is sometimes used in its place.

**Shocked quartz**
A variety of quartz with planar deformation features formed by sudden extreme pressure, as in meteorite impacts and nuclear bomb tests. It is found at the Chicxulub crater, Barringer (Meteor) Crater, and in the K-T (Cretaceous-Paleogene) boundary layer, where, together with an iridium anomaly, it supports the Alvarez hypothesis that an asteroid impact killed the dinosaurs.

**Amethyst and citrine**
The two most frequently named colored varieties of quartz: amethyst is purple and citrine is yellow to orange, a color traced to iron impurities; heating amethyst can produce citrine. Ametrine is a single crystal with both purple amethyst and orange citrine zones.

**Other varieties: rose, smoky, milky, onyx, Tiger's Eye, prasiolite**
Quartz comes in many named varieties. Rose quartz is pink, smoky quartz is brown-gray (its color is linked to aluminum impurities and natural irradiation), and milky quartz is white. Prasiolite (also sold as vermarine) is a rare green variety, and aventurine is quartz with glittering mica inclusions.

**Tiger's Eye and chatoyancy**
A golden-brown variety of quartz with fibrous inclusions (originally crocidolite) that shows chatoyancy, the "cat's eye" effect, a band of light that moves across the stone as it is turned.

**Goldich dissolution series**
Quartz sits at the bottom of this series ranking minerals by their susceptibility to chemical weathering, meaning it is the most resistant. This durability explains why quartz dominates sand and sandstone.

**Second most abundant mineral in Earth's crust (after feldspar)**
Quartz is the second most common mineral in the continental crust, after feldspar. Granite is composed mainly of feldspar and quartz, and quartz is the main component of sandstone and of its metamorphic counterpart, quartzite.

**Chalcedony, agate, chert, and flint**
These are microcrystalline or cryptocrystalline forms of quartz. Chalcedony is a waxy intergrowth of quartz and its polymorph moganite, and agate, onyx, jasper, chert, and flint are all composed of very fine-grained quartz.

**Coesite, stishovite, tridymite, and cristobalite**
Other polymorphs of SiO2 with the same composition but different crystal structures. Coesite and stishovite are dense high-pressure forms found in meteorite impact craters, while tridymite and cristobalite are high-temperature forms.

**Alpha-beta transition at 573 degrees Celsius**
Ordinary trigonal alpha quartz converts to hexagonal beta (high) quartz at 573 degrees Celsius (846 K). The sudden volume change during this inversion can cause dunting (cracking) in quartz-rich pottery clay during kiln firing.

**Herkimer diamonds**
Despite their name, these are clear, doubly terminated quartz crystals (pointed at both ends), named after Herkimer County, New York.

**Conchoidal fracture and Nicolas Steno**
Quartz breaks with a smooth, curved conchoidal fracture, like obsidian, rather than cleaving along flat planes. By studying quartz crystals, Nicolas Steno discovered that the angles between corresponding crystal faces are always the same, the law of constancy of interfacial angles.
